AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards

Xin Gao2,∗  Yifan Yang1,†  Xin Li3  Pan Wang4  Yan Li5  Muzhao Tian6
Mingxi Cheng1  Bei Liu1  Kai Qiu1  Qi Dai1  Dong Chen1  Yue Dong1
Leandros Tassiulas2,†  Rex Ying2,†  Ji Li1  Chong Luo1

1 Microsoft    2 Yale University    3 Nanyang Technological University
4 University of Pittsburgh    5 Shanghai Jiao Tong University    6 Fudan University

Introduction

Information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards pack dense content into a single canvas [29, 45]. Generating them as code is highly desirable because the output remains structured, editable, and verifiable. However, code models suffer from a fundamental limitation: they cannot “see” the canvas. Spatial layout, hierarchy, and color are declared line by line, resulting in outputs that satisfy content constraints but often appear visually dated. In contrast, image generators excel at composing visually striking pages [8, 10], yet frequently misrender text, numbers, and logical relations, producing raster outputs that cannot be edited or verified [23, 37].

These complementary strengths motivate a novel setting where an image generator provides an aesthetic guidance for the code model. Specifically, a reference image generated from the same prompt serves as a conditional input to supply layout and style inspiration. While existing image-to-code methods [1, 36, 14] also use images as input, they treat them as absolute ground truth for pixel-level reconstruction. This rigid replication and its associated image-level metrics [6, 42, 21] fail in our setting because they force the code model to mimic the hallucinated content of the generated prior and penalize valid design variations. Our fundamental setting therefore challenges the code model to strictly satisfy the prompt’s content while flexibly extracting layout and style from a noisy reference image.

Simply providing the reference image as an input is insufficient. Off-the-shelf vision-language models (VLMs) naturally entangle visual features with text semantics. When given a noisy reference, they tend to either reproduce its hallucinated content or ignore its layout entirely. The model therefore requires explicit training to extract the aesthetic prior while adhering to the text prompt. To facilitate this, we propose AesCode, which conceptualizes the generated target as a Design Graph. This structured intermediate representation explicitly separates semantic information from visual cues. Within this graph, nodes represent distinct functional elements such as text blocks, tables, and charts. Each node possesses decoupled attributes for its required content (e.g., specific strings or data series) and its visual properties (e.g., bounding boxes and colors). Edges explicitly define structural relationships, including hierarchical containment and spatial alignment.

Because the graph structure makes individual properties explicitly attributable, it naturally enables decoupled reward channels tailored to distinct objectives. Blending mixed outcomes into a single score (e.g., rendering correct text but a chaotic layout) often misaligns training gradients. To preserve specific learning signals, we derive synergic cross-modal rewards directly from the graph: deterministic verifiers provide fast, absolute checks for properties readable from code and DOM rendering, while a VLM judge assesses aesthetics through a Visual Graph Rubric (VGR), avoiding unstable holistic scoring by answering node-specific binary questions. We then balance these channels using Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) [24], preventing dense verification signals from overwhelming sparse aesthetic feedback.

We also release an infographic benchmark evaluating verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with automated visual scores closely matching human judgments. Ablations confirm that reference images consistently improve visual quality as an aesthetic prior across all tested models. Given the same references, our AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B gain 31.1 and 22.4 Visual points over their Qwen3-VL backbones, achieving visual quality comparable to frontier models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 while making noticeably fewer content errors.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a novel paradigm for aesthetic code generation that utilizes image generators as an aesthetic prior. A reference image generated from the same prompt conditions the code model as input and provides visual signals during training.

  • •

    We propose AesCode, which introduces decoupled cross-modal rewards driven by a design graph. It pairs deterministic verifiers for structural correctness with a sample-specific, graph-based VLM judge for aesthetic quality.

  • •

    We release an infographic benchmark that evaluates correctness and visual quality separately, with human-aligned visual scores. References help every model we test, and AesCode matches leading proprietary models visually while following the prompt more closely.

Related Work

Visual Design and Code Generation. Posters, slides, and infographics can be generated as images or code. Image generators such as PosterMaker [10] and BizGen [30] compose appealing pages, but still misrender text and data on dense content [37], and their raster outputs cannot be edited. Code is editable and verifiable. When written from text alone, as in LIDA [7] and PPTAgent [45], it is composed without seeing the page and often looks plain. When written from an image, as in Design2Code [36] and ChartMimic [41], it copies the input as ground truth. Closest to ours, DesignAsCode [26] and Editable Visual Design [43] let a coding agent consult a generated image, but only at inference time; the code model is never trained to use it. We instead train the code model to follow a prompt-generated image as an aesthetic prior for layout and style.

Reward Design for Visual Generation. RL training requires a reward for the rendered page. In image-to-code, this reward is usually similarity to the input image, measured with visual metrics [33, 3] or MLLM critics [42, 21]. For a generated reference, however, this would penalize valid alternatives and reward copied errors. Without a target image, rule-based rewards are precise but limited to what a program can check, such as element overlap in AeSlides [28], while holistic MLLM judges [46, 2] give scores that shift with prompt phrasing. A more stable alternative breaks one judgment into many yes/no questions, first for text-to-image evaluation [4] and more recently as rubric rewards for RL [12, 31]. These questions, however, are derived from text alone and cannot check the design a reference proposes. We therefore build a design graph from the prompt and the reference, verify code-level properties with rules, and turn the remaining visual properties into a Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements.

Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning. Critic-free methods such as GRPO [35] normalize rewards within a sampled group and, following DeepSeek-R1 [13], have become a standard recipe for post-training LLMs and VLMs [25]. They assume a single reward, however: when several rewards are summed before normalization, a dense, near-saturated rule reward can drown out a sparse aesthetic one. MO-GRPO [16] reweights rewards by their variance, while GDPO [24] normalizes each reward separately. We adopt GDPO to balance our rule-based and VGR rewards.

Appendix A extends this review with a fuller discussion of each of the three threads above.

Method

AesCode learns visual design through graph-structured supervision. We first construct a target design graph that combines prompt-required content with non-authoritative reference cues (Section 3.1). We then route its properties to deterministic and perceptual reward channels (Section 3.2) and optimize them with SFT and GDPO [24] (Section 3.3). Finally, we define a separate evaluation protocol for factual correctness and human-aligned visual quality (Section 3.4).

Design Graph as a Supervision Target

The prompt pp specifies required information, while visual design admits many valid solutions. Learning needs a concrete signal, so an image generator supplies one compelling possibility IrefI_{\mathrm{ref}}, which may be factually or structurally wrong. We therefore organize supervision as a design graph rather than a monolithic target, scoring prompt-derived requirements independently of the reference.

We define the supervision target as

𝒢tgt=(𝒱,ℰ,𝐗V,r)=Φ⁡(p,Iref),\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}_{V},r)=\Phi(p,I_{\mathrm{ref}}), (1)

where the canvas root rr holds page-level attributes and contains every top-level element. The remaining nodes come from a closed vocabulary of atomic elements, such as text, images, charts, tables, and badges, and of containers, such as regions, cards, panels, lists, and groups, which hold other nodes instead of rendering content; three or more interchangeable siblings collapse into one group node with a count attribute. Attributes 𝐗V\mathbf{X}_{V} record content, geometry, and appearance, including structured chart and table data, and each edge (u,τ,v)∈ℰ(u,\tau,v)\in\mathcal{E} carries a relation type τ\tau covering containment, alignment, order, adjacency, and semantic connection. This decomposition lets prompt requirements and reference cues constrain complementary properties independently, making supervision attributable across semantic dimensions, and since it assumes only elements and their two-dimensional structure, it applies broadly to structured visual artifacts.

From the generated code cc and its rendering I^\hat{I}, we jointly parse all candidate visual elements into 𝒢^=Ψ⁡(c,I^)\hat{\mathcal{G}}=\Psi(c,\hat{I}). Code, DOM, and computed styles expose structured content and implementation details, while the rendering provides pixel geometry and visual evidence. We then compare 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}} with 𝒢tgt\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}} property by property to derive the reward signals below.

From Design Graphs to Multi-Objective Rewards

Graph properties divide by how they can be assessed. Those with structured evidence in code or measurable evidence in the rendering are programmatically verifiable, while appearance and higher-order relations vary by sample and require visual judgment. We therefore use deterministic verifiers and a sample-specific VLM-as-judge channel, detailed in Appendix D.

Deterministic verifiers. Six verifiers compute scores from code, the DOM, OCR, and rendered pixels. Execution (sexecs_{\mathrm{exec}}) checks renderability and fatal errors. Text (stexts_{\mathrm{text}}) verifies required strings, and Boundary (sbdrys_{\mathrm{bdry}}) measures canvas containment and aspect-ratio agreement. Table/Chart (stcs_{\mathrm{tc}}) parses the structure, subtype, and data of HTML tables and ECharts charts, preventing static substitutes from receiving credit. Semantic Layout (slayouts_{\mathrm{layout}}) matches OCR text blocks between reference and candidate and scores their normalized positional agreement. Whitespace (swss_{\mathrm{ws}}) compares non-background occupancy at coarse and fine scales, capturing how whitespace is distributed.

Visual Graph Rubric (svgrs_{\mathrm{vgr}}). For the remaining properties, we derive a sample-specific list of Boolean questions QtrainQ_{\mathrm{train}} from 𝒢tgt\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}}. Each question binds to a node, attribute, relation, or subgraph, so the graph scaffolds rubric construction rather than serving as a policy input, turning open-ended visual judgment into explicit criteria. A VLM answers the fixed questions from the candidate rendering, and their pass rate gives

svgr=1|Qtrain|​∑q∈Qtrain[I^​satisfies​q].s_{\mathrm{vgr}}=\tfrac{1}{|Q_{\mathrm{train}}|}\sum\nolimits_{q\in Q_{\mathrm{train}}}\mathbb{1}\!\left[\hat{I}\ \text{satisfies}\ q\right]. (2)

Reference cues enter only through fixed questions, and VGR is used only for training.

Training Pipeline

Cold-start SFT first establishes reliable prompt-and-image-to-code generation from filtered teacher demonstrations paired with the collected images. RL then switches to image-generator references and optimizes the seven rewards. These channels differ in applicability, scale, sparsity, saturation, and learning difficulty, so aggregating raw rewards can obscure useful signals. We therefore use Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) [24].

For each (p,Iref)(p,I_{\mathrm{ref}}), we sample code rollouts ℬ={ci}i=1B\mathcal{B}=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}, render I^i=render⁡(ci)\hat{I}_{i}=\operatorname{render}(c_{i}), and parse 𝒢^i=Ψ⁡(ci,I^i)\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{i}=\Psi(c_{i},\hat{I}_{i}). Comparing 𝒢^i\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{i} with 𝒢tgt\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}} produces the seven rewards above as 𝐬i=(si(v))v=17∈[0,1]7\mathbf{s}_{i}=(s_{i}^{(v)})_{v=1}^{7}\in[0,1]^{7}. A mask mi(v)∈{0,1}m_{i}^{(v)}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether channel vv applies to rollout ii. Let μv\mu_{v} and σv\sigma_{v} denote its mean and standard deviation over the applicable subset ℬv={i∣mi(v)=1}\mathcal{B}_{v}=\{i\mid m_{i}^{(v)}=1\}. GDPO normalizes each channel before averaging the applicable advantages:

Ai(v)=si(v)−μvσv+ϵ,Ai=∑vmi(v)​Ai(v)∑vmi(v).A_{i}^{(v)}=\tfrac{s_{i}^{(v)}-\mu_{v}}{\sigma_{v}+\epsilon},\qquad A_{i}=\tfrac{\sum\nolimits_{v}m_{i}^{(v)}A_{i}^{(v)}}{\sum\nolimits_{v}m_{i}^{(v)}}. (3)

With ρi​(θ)=πθ​(ci∣p,Iref)/πold​(ci∣p,Iref)\rho_{i}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(c_{i}\mid p,I_{\mathrm{ref}})/\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(c_{i}\mid p,I_{\mathrm{ref}}), GDPO maximizes the clipped group objective

ℒGDPO​(θ)=1B​∑i=1Bmin⁡(ρi​(θ)​Ai,clip⁡(ρi​(θ),1−ε,1+ε)​Ai).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GDPO}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{B}\min\!\left(\rho_{i}(\theta)A_{i},\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\rho_{i}(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon\bigr)A_{i}\right). (4)

Applicability masks exclude irrelevant checks, so all valid objectives contribute to one policy update without first collapsing their raw rewards into a scalar.

Final Evaluation Protocol

Training requires a concrete reference, but evaluation must accept multiple valid designs. We therefore assess the artifact itself through Rule, Visual, and their mean Overall.

Rule. Rule averages Text, Boundary, and Table/Chart (Section 3.2), which verify exact content, canvas containment, and structured data from code and rendering.

Visual. Visual converts open-ended, sample-specific quality into a checklist QpQ_{p} derived from prompt requirements. Content checks required-element presence and completeness; Layout covers organization, relations, and collisions; and Style judges hierarchy, typography, color, and component finish against a production-ready standard. Each checklist averages 35.8 questions. A VLM answers fixed yes/no questions from the candidate rendering, and Visual averages the three dimensions. These are absolute criteria for the artifact rather than pairwise comparisons. We develop the pipeline on a separate 50-instance set: it drafts questions, filters ambiguous, non-visual, and implementation-specific criteria, then revises wording and coverage. Annotators review questions and rank output pairs; ranking disagreements guide each revision. Once consistency exceeds 90%90\% and no issues remain, we freeze the pipeline and apply it unchanged to the disjoint 300-instance benchmark, giving every system the same sample-specific criteria. Appendix E details the pipeline, while Section E.3 confirms strong agreement with human aesthetic judgments and pairwise choices.

Experiments

Experimental Setup

Training data. We curate a candidate pool of approximately 18,000 human-designed slides, posters, dashboards, and webpages, clustered by their CLIP image features. For each sampled image, GPT-5.4-mini infers a generation prompt that specifies required contents (e.g., text and charts) without prescribing visual layout or styles. For SFT, we construct 3,000 demonstrations using GPT-5.5 paired with the original human designs. We generate three rollouts per prompt–image pair and keep the highest-scoring candidate if its reward exceeds 0.850.85, otherwise resampling from the same cluster. Retaining original designs for SFT teaches the prompt-and-reference-to-code format without image-generation overhead. For RL, we score eight rollouts from the cold-start policy on every remaining prompt, keep the prompts whose pass​@​1\text{pass}@1 and pass​@​8\text{pass}@8 rates leave usable learning signal, rebalance them across clusters, and replace the original images with synthetic references from GPT-Image-2, yielding roughly 8,000 prompts. See details in Section B.1.

Benchmark and baselines. Our test set for benchmarking contains 300 prompts, with GPT-Image-2 references (Section B.3). We compare proprietary and open-source models under prompt-only and reference-conditioned settings. Final evaluation follows the protocol in Section 3.4 (detailed checklist construction and a complete example checklist appear in Section E.1). We additionally evaluate Design2Code [36], SlidesBench [11], and GDB/lica [5] using their respective protocols (Section E.2).

Implementation details. AesCode uses Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B, with SFT at a learning rate of 10−510^{-5} followed by GDPO using AdamW at 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}. Each RL step samples 128128 prompts with 88 rollouts each; the 8B and 32B models train for 400400 and 520520 steps, respectively. Remaining optimization, decoding, and rendering settings appear in Section C.1.

Main Results

Main observations. Table 1 reveals three main observations. First, reference images improve visual presentation for all closed and open models by providing explicit layout and aesthetic anchors. Yet, Style remains a shared bottleneck below 60%60\%: this metric gives credit only when a design requires no further visual revision before production delivery. Second, models leverage visual guidance differently. Claude Opus 4.8 excels in content fidelity and uses references to elevate layout and style, whereas GPT-5.5 starts with stronger style and benefits most in content and layout. Most open models are highly imbalanced: some satisfy code-level constraints but remain weak visually, while others struggle on both. Qwen3.8 and Qwen3.5 stand out for more balanced visual planning, with Qwen3.8 showing the best balance between Rule and Visual among the open models evaluated. Its relatively high prompt-only Visual score leaves limited room for further gains from an additional reference (73.15→75.7273.15\to 75.72). Third, our training substantially improves both base backbones, raising Overall from 51.9351.93 to 82.9482.94 at 8B and from 61.1061.10 to 85.8985.89 at 32B. The 32B model also leads Table/Chart at 90.3790.37. We require tables to use HTML table structures and charts to use ECharts, which constrains the solution space to executable, directly verifiable implementations and provides clear rewards for optimization. Overall, AesCode leads in verifiable correctness while matching frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 in visual quality.

Case studies.

Figure 3 illustrates why frontier models can still trail AesCode despite plausible overall compositions. GPT-5.5 overlooks a subtle headline overlap, renders four rather than five requested logo slots, and lets a message band obscure a correctly instantiated ECharts chart. The last case retains a full Chart score because its structure and data are present; the failure lies in rendered visibility and is captured by Content and Layout. Together, these cases expose weaknesses in overlap control, requirement completeness, and the visual realization of valid code.

Transfer to external benchmarks.

Across three benchmarks with different tasks and metrics, AesCode-32B improves on its Qwen3-VL-32B backbone in all fourteen measures, demonstrating transfer beyond our benchmark. The largest gains appear on design-sensitive measures, including SlidesBench layout and color and GDB/lica NIMA, FID, and color harmony. Gains are smaller on Design2Code, an older website-reconstruction benchmark whose similarity metrics are near saturation and align less closely with human aesthetic judgments (Figure 5). Thus, GPT-5.5 remains stronger in exact screenshot fidelity, while AesCode shows that its transferable gains lie in layout and visual design rather than reconstruction-specific similarity.

Ablation Study

Reference conditioning during training and inference.

Table 4 shows that reference-conditioned training internalizes multimodal visual planning into the policy. Removing the reference only at inference reduces AesCode-8B Visual by 1.001.00 point, compared with 19.5519.55 for its backbone and 10.0410.04 for GPT-5.5. Even when the policy never sees the reference, reference-based rewards raise prompt-only Visual from 25.1725.17 to 69.7169.71, showing that such supervision transfers visual capability indirectly. This remains 5.095.09 points below reference-conditioned training under the same inference setting, confirming the value of the reference as an input condition.

Training and reward design.

Table 4 shows that RL drives most gains, while SFT gives a stronger initialization: under the same RL budget, Overall rises from 77.9777.97 to 82.9482.94. GDPO adds 5.125.12 Visual points over scalar GRPO by normalizing channels independently, which helps when verifiable and perceptual objectives learn at different rates (Section C.2). Design supervision then determines visual quality: code correctness alone yields 66.5966.59 Visual, and Layout/Whitespace raises it to 68.1268.12. CLIP reaches 70.4970.49 through coarse image-level guidance but cannot localize failed properties, while a holistic VLM score reaches only 68.9168.91 because its absolute signal is sparse and unstable. VGR decomposes visual quality into explicit graph-bound criteria and reaches 75.8075.80 without sacrificing Rule. Graph construction accounts for part of this: with the same inputs and training setup, authoring the questions directly, without the graph, lowers Visual to 72.6172.61 at unchanged Rule (90.0790.07 vs. 90.0590.05).

Analysis

Human evaluation. Our blinded human study validates the automatic judges and the main comparison (Section E.3). In Figure 5a, human-majority judgments agree with the training VGR and the Visual checklist on 89.3% and 93.3% of sampled predicates. In Figure 5b, AesCode-32B achieves higher Content satisfaction than GPT-5.5 (86.50% vs. 83.47%) with equivalent aesthetic quality (mean difference −0.15-0.15, 95% CI [−0.34,0.03][-0.34,0.03] within the pre-specified ±0.5\pm 0.5 margin). In Figure 5c, our Visual score agrees with direct human pairwise choices in 80.66% of comparisons, exceeds external metrics across comparable gap bins, and improves with larger score gaps.

Failure analysis. Lower-performing samples show three recurring failure modes (Figure 5). First, canvas overflow persists, though it is rare after training: code generation cannot reliably anticipate final pixel geometry, leaving visually grounded refinement to future work. Second, relational structure is harder than individual elements, since the model must understand content relations and render them as spatial connections, yet relation-level rewards stay sparse and do not localize the failed edge. Third, semantic elements often degrade into generic marks, since such icons require fine-grained SVG drawing grounded in meaning.

Conclusion

This work asks how code models can generate information-rich visual artifacts that are both verifiable and visually compelling. We address this challenge by representing each target as a design graph that captures element content, visual attributes, and relations. Prompt requirements define what must be conveyed, while image-generated references guide how it should look; together, they yield targeted rewards that help compact code models internalize cross-modal understanding, organization, and visual judgment. AesCode matches frontier systems in human-aligned visual quality and surpasses them in verifiable correctness, with much of this capability retained even without reference input at inference. More broadly, our results show that image generators can serve not only as content generators, but also as scalable teachers of visual design for structured generative models. Remaining challenges in pixel-level geometry, complex relations, and semantic visual elements call for visually grounded iterative refinement and more precise structural feedback.

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Visual design and code generation. Image generators now produce product posters [10] and article-level infographics [30], and COLE [17] assembles multi-layered designs from a pipeline of specialized models rather than general-purpose code. On dense infographics, however, they still distort data encodings and misspell strings [37], and even a correct output is a raster that cannot be edited or checked element by element. Generating code avoids this. Text-to-code methods write visualization code [7], layouts [9], or slides [11, 45], but compose the page without seeing it. Image-to-code methods recover the code behind a rendered webpage [1, 20, 36], chart [39, 41], or SVG [32]. Because the input is the rendering of an existing program, a closer copy is always a better answer.

The closest work combines an image model with code at inference time. PosterVerse renders HTML typography over a generated background [22], DesignAsCode uses an image-editing model to propose an improved render during reflection [26], and, concurrently, Editable Visual Design lets a coding agent use a generated visual as a global reference for composition and color [43]. In each case, the image steers a prompted pipeline, and the code model is never trained to use it. AesCode instead trains the code model to follow a prompt-generated reference as an aesthetic prior while ignoring its content errors, and turns the same reference into a training signal.

Reward design for visual generation. Image-to-code RL rewards a rollout by how closely its render matches the input image, using visual similarity [3, 33] or MLLM critics [6, 42, 21]. This is valid only when the input is an exact target. A generated reference is not: many programs realize the same prompt, and the generator may alter requested content. Without a target image, rule-based rewards such as layout metrics for slides [28] are stable but cover only what a program can decide. Preference-trained reward models [40, 19] capture subjective quality but inherit labeler noise. Holistic MLLM judges [46, 2] need no training, but their scores vary with prompt phrasing, and when used as an aesthetic reward, as in WebGen-R1 [18], they reflect general quality rather than what suits a particular prompt.

Judgments become more reliable when split into narrow yes/no questions. TIFA [15] and DSG [4] do so for text-to-image evaluation, ArtifactsBench uses per-task checklists to evaluate rendered artifacts [44], and instruction-derived rubrics now serve as RL rewards for language models [38, 12] and, concurrently, for SVG [31]. All of these derive their questions from text alone. Our Visual Graph Rubric derives them from a design graph of both the prompt and the reference, so it can check the layout and style the reference proposes, and each failure points to a specific element. Properties a program can decide are left to rule-based verifiers.

Multi-objective reinforcement learning. Post-training RL has moved from PPO [34, 27] to critic-free, group-normalized methods such as GRPO [35], and we follow the R1-style recipe of a supervised cold start followed by such RL [13, 25]. With seven reward channels, summing them before group normalization lets their different scales and firing rates interfere, so a dense, near-saturated channel can suppress a sparse but informative one. MO-GRPO reweights rewards by their variance [16], while GDPO normalizes each channel separately [24]. We adopt GDPO because our channels differ widely in how often they fire and how much they vary.

Appendix B Data and Benchmark Construction

Source Designs and Stratified Sampling

Every split is built from human-designed graphics, because content is what they supply best: the text has a reason to be there, the sections stand in a sensible relation to one another, and the reading order reflects an actual communicative intent. Prompts and verifiable requirements are therefore inferred from human designs for the SFT, RL, and benchmark splits alike. Visual style is a separate matter. Designs that are modern and polished in every respect are a small and unevenly distributed minority of the collected pool, so the style of a given source image is largely an accident of where it was sampled from.

This separation decides which image the policy sees as its reference. Cold-start SFT shows the original human design, since that stage only establishes the prompt-and-image-to-code format. RL and the benchmark instead show a reference that an image generator produces from the inferred prompt. This is the input the method is built for: at deployment, an image generator turns a design intent into one concrete visual proposal, and a code model implements that proposal as markup. A generated reference supplies a uniform contemporary register, but it is one sample from a generator and need not agree with its prompt in every string or ordering. Training and evaluating on human designs would tune the policy to an input it never receives at deployment.

We collect approximately 18,000 human-designed slides, posters, dashboards, and webpages, extract CLIP image features, and cluster the pool. Distances from each cluster center are divided into equal-width intervals, and each sampling round draws equal numbers of samples from these intervals without replacement, so that peripheral designs are covered as well as those near the centers. Strata too sparse to support the allocation are excluded. Because sources are drawn without replacement, the SFT, RL, and benchmark splits are disjoint; Section B.4 checks this directly on the released files.

Most of the pool comes from public design collections released under the MIT and Apache-2.0 licenses; the remainder is internal data used for training only. We do not release the source images. We release the artifacts our pipeline produces: the inferred prompts, the verifiable requirements, the generated reference images, and the generated markup and renderings of every evaluated arm. Since the references are generated from text prompts rather than copied from the source designs, the release contains everything needed to reproduce the RL setup and the benchmark without redistributing the underlying collections.

Prompt Inference and SFT Demonstrations

GPT-5.4-mini infers a generation prompt from each sampled image. The prompt specifies the artifact type and its content, including required text, charts, and data, and names the major layout zones and the reading flow, since a request that lists content without saying how it is organized does not describe a deliverable. It may carry one coarse register cue, such as a warm or cool palette, but prescribes none of the appearance choices the visual channels supervise: no specific colors, component shapes, spacing, or typography. The image supplies that guidance. The requirement record extracted alongside the prompt is stricter and admits only exact strings, chart data, and table data. We call such a prompt content-only.

To build SFT data, GPT-5.5 receives the prompt together with the original human design and writes three HTML candidates. We render and score them with our reward system and keep the highest-scoring candidate if its reward exceeds 0.850.85; clusters left below their allocation are resampled. This yields 3,000 demonstrations, each storing the prompt, the original image, the selected code, and the requirements. No image generator is called at this stage.

Figure B1 shows one demonstration. Because the supervision target is markup, a demonstration is a triple rather than a pair: the source design the prompt was inferred from, the markup the loss is computed on, and the render the reward system scored during filtering. The excerpt also shows the properties the rule checks depend on. The page is a fixed artboard at the requested canvas size, every visible string lives in its own text node, and icons are built from styled elements rather than fetched as assets, so a render can be read back and checked against the item’s requirements.

RL and Benchmark References

For the pool remaining after SFT construction, we infer content-only prompts and select the RL set by difficulty. The cold-start policy generates eight rollouts per prompt, and the reward system of Appendix D scores each one, giving a pass@1 and a pass@8 rate per prompt without additional annotation. Prompts solved on nearly every rollout carry little gradient signal under a group-normalized objective, and prompts failed on every rollout carry none, so we keep the band in which pass@1 and pass@8 separate. The retained prompts are then rebalanced across CLIP clusters so that the difficulty filter does not concentrate the RL set in whichever artifact type the SFT policy found hardest. This yields 7,4087{,}408 RL prompts, shared by both backbones. GPT-Image-2 generates a new reference from each prompt, and the original human design is never shown to the policy.

The held-out benchmark contains 300 items drawn across the four artifact types and the CLIP clusters, with no source design shared with SFT or RL. Prompts and references are constructed exactly as for RL, and the original designs are not used at test time. Each item is stored independently of any model output and contains the natural-language request, format and canvas metadata, atomic verifiable requirements, the prompt-derived evaluation checklist, and the reference.

All systems receive the same prompt and reference wherever their interface supports image conditioning. We generate three rollouts per prompt and average their scores without selection. Rendering failures remain in the denominator, and Execution is reported only as a diagnostic, excluded from Rule, Visual, and Overall. The non-conditional experiments in Table 4 use the same items and scoring and differ only in whether IrefI_{\mathrm{ref}} is shown to the policy.

Dataset Statistics

Table B1 summarizes the three splits. Since sampling is stratified over 2525 CLIP clusters rather than over a declared artifact label, the benchmark is balanced by cluster, with 99 to 2020 items per cluster. Canvas shape is inherited from the source design. A benchmark item carries a median of 1212 verifiable requirements (range 33 to 2323); the count follows how much legible, checkable content the source contains, because the extraction template prefers fewer high-confidence requirements over broader but noisier ones. We verify split disjointness directly: the 300300 benchmark identifiers have an empty intersection with the RL training file. Twenty-seven benchmark items were drawn from the RL candidate pool and are labeled as such in the release, but they were removed from that pool when drawn and do not appear in the training file.

Figure B2 shows six benchmark items. What an item asks for is fixed by its prompt and requirements, while the reference supplies visual guidance and is never the object of a string-level check. The items are multilingual and mix canvas shapes, both inherited from the source pool.

Prompts Used for Data Construction

Two model calls stand between a source design and a usable training item. The first reads the source image and returns the generation prompt together with its verifiable requirements; the second turns that prompt into a reference image. We print the first template in full, since it carries the contract the reward depends on, and describe the second in prose.

The first call produces the prompt and the requirements in a single JSON object rather than extracting requirements from the prompt afterwards, and it forbids any text_exact requirement whose string does not appear exactly in the generation prompt. A requirement is thus a marked verification point inside the prompt, not an independent claim about the source image, and a model that follows the prompt cannot be penalized for a string it was never asked to produce. The template keeps style at the level of one coarse category cue, which leaves palette, typography, and decoration to the reference image. Two further rules exist because the target is code: charts must be requested as ECharts with literal data arrays, since otherwise a static picture of a chart would be an acceptable reading of the prompt, and content HTML cannot draw, such as photographs and brand logos, must be requested as a sized placehold.co slot.

The second call generates the reference image with GPT-Image-2. The prompt cannot be passed through unchanged, because it was written for a code generator: a placehold.co slot tells the model to leave a region empty, and constraints such as CSS-only icons or no photographs exist only because HTML cannot draw them. Passing these through would make the reference inherit the limitations of the code target. A deterministic rewrite therefore turns each placeholder request into a description of the illustration it stands for and drops the code-only constraints and pixel sizing, while leaving layout structure, text, and chart and table values untouched, so that the reference and the requirements still describe the same artifact. A fixed prefix then asks for a contemporary editorial register and fully drawn illustrations. This instruction applies to the reference only: the code prompt still requests placeholder slots, and the judge counts a placeholder as the image being present. The canvas follows the aspect ratio of the source design, rounded to a multiple of 1616.

Appendix C Implementation and Additional Results

This section gives the settings needed to reproduce a run and the results that support the main text. All scores use the Rule and Visual columns of Table 1.

Implementation Details

Training configuration.

AesCode uses Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B backbones. Cold-start SFT uses the 3,000 demonstrations above with a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, followed by GDPO on the same 7,4087{,}408 RL prompts for both scales, so that the two backbones differ only in capacity. We use verl’s FSDP–vLLM hybrid engine without a critic or a separately trained reward model. RL uses AdamW with a constant learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}, no warmup, and weight decay 0.010.01. Each step samples 128 prompts with eight rollouts each and runs one optimization epoch; the 8B and 32B models are trained for 400 and 520 steps. KL regularization is applied in the loss rather than the reward, with KL and entropy coefficients both 0.0010.001. Rollouts use temperature 1.01.0 and top-pp 1.01.0, with prompt and response each capped at 8,192 tokens.

Inference and decoding.

Benchmark generation uses three rollouts per prompt with temperature 0.80.8, top-pp 0.950.95, at most 12,000 output tokens, and a model context of 24,576 tokens. Closed-source baselines are queried through their hosted APIs with the same prompt and rollout count. Reasoning-mode endpoints do not accept sampling parameters and run at provider defaults; the other hosted arms use 0.80.8 and 0.950.95. No arm is tuned on our benchmark. All generations were collected between 28 August and 18 September 2026, and we release the generated markup and renderings of every arm.

Rendering sandbox.

Candidate HTML is rendered from a local file in a sandboxed Playwright browser. The canvas size comes from the reference metadata, with 1280×7201280\times 720 used only when it is absent; the viewport is enlarged when necessary and the screenshot is clipped to the canvas. ECharts and placeholder assets are served locally, and other external requests are blocked. The renderer exports the DOM, computed styles, bounding boxes, console status, and the screenshot, and a 120-second safeguard recycles stalled workers.

Learning Dynamics of the Decoupled Reward Channels

Figure C1 shows that Execution saturates after cold-start SFT, while Text and Chart improve fastest (pass@1 from ≈0.79\approx\!0.79 to ≈0.94\approx\!0.94 and from ≈0.58\approx\!0.58 to ≈0.87\approx\!0.87). The design channels improve more slowly and are still rising when training ends, consistent with spatial and perceptual organization being harder to acquire. Boundary stabilizes early with low within-group variance, precisely the kind of signal that scalar aggregation would suppress. Pass@1 converges toward pass@8, so RL makes behavior that previously appeared only in the best rollouts typical of a single sample, and the close training and held-out curves show no visible reward trade-off or overfitting.

Loss of Verifiable Capabilities under Reconstruction Objectives

A natural alternative to the decoupled reward is to score a rollout by how closely its render reproduces the reference. Table C1 evaluates this alternative under the same checklist, columns, and aggregation as Table 1; the lower block fixes the backbone, training prompts, and sampler and varies only the reward.

A reconstruction scalar does move the visual dimensions it can see: CLIP-similarity GRPO raises Layout from 71.1971.19 to 78.4578.45 and Visual from 60.1160.11 to 65.6965.69, and an absolute VLM score moves them in the same direction by a smaller margin. It does not preserve capabilities that are discrete and checkable. Chart falls from 42.3542.35 on the backbone to 9.679.67, 9.789.78, and 15.2715.27 across the three reconstruction arms, and the cause is visible in the markup. Among the 8989 prompts with a chart_data or table_data requirement, we count a prompt as charted if any of its rollouts calls echarts.init, since loading the library without instantiating a chart yields exactly the static substitute at issue. The backbone charts 7373 prompts and AesCode-8B 8080, whereas the reconstruction arms chart only 1515, 88, and 2626, replacing the rest with static markup that is close in pixels and wrong in content. Published image-to-code systems show the same pattern, with UI2Coden at 7.567.56 Chart despite a Visual score of 59.9259.92. A similarity scalar cannot separate a real chart from a picture of one.

Additional Qualitative Results

Figures C2 and C3 show a random sample of AesCode-32B outputs, complementing the side-by-side comparison in Figure 3 at a size where the pages can be read. Each panel is a single rollout on a randomly drawn held-out benchmark prompt, rendered in the evaluation sandbox and shown unedited. The sample covers dashboards with live charts, diagrams, slides, and tall posters, in several languages, with no per-format change to the prompt or decoding.

Appendix D Reward System

This section specifies each training reward of Section 3.2. Reference-side evidence comes from the prompt, its requirements, and IrefI_{\mathrm{ref}}; element correspondences use text, type, semantic role, and relative geometry, and no verifier requires pixel-perfect reconstruction. Figure D1 summarizes the seven channels. These rewards supply the learning signal only; the reported scores are defined separately in Appendix E.

Per-Rollout Reward Record

Every rollout produces a structured record rather than a single scalar. For each channel vv the record holds an applicability mask mv∈{0,1}m_{v}\in\{0,1\}, a raw score sv∈[0,1]s_{v}\in[0,1], and a diagnostic payload eve_{v} (Table D1). Results marked not applicable are excluded from aggregation, whereas explicit zero-score failures are included. Infrastructure failures are recorded separately from semantic ones, so a judge timeout is never read as negative design feedback, and the same record serves training curves, benchmark aggregation, and qualitative diagnosis.

Verifiable Requirements

Verifiable requirements are extracted from the prompt before generation and do not depend on any candidate output. The schema has three types: text_exact retains the exact required string, and chart_data and table_data retain the expected object type, labels, series, and values. Canvas metadata supplies the target dimensions used by Boundary. Pairwise and group relations are not part of this schema; graph-bound VGR predicates supervise them during training, and the prompt-derived Visual checklist evaluates them at test time.

Deterministic Verifiers

Execution.

Playwright aborts external requests outside the allowlist, and the static resource audit records violations without a direct penalty. Empty HTML and render blockers receive zero. A render is blank when its grayscale variance is below 8.08.0 and its dark-pixel ratio below 0.0050.005, and renders exceeding 15,00015{,}000 ms also fail. After network and instrumentation errors are filtered, NfatalN_{\mathrm{fatal}} uncaught JavaScript errors give sexec=exp⁡(−0.4​Nfatal)s_{\mathrm{exec}}=\exp(-0.4N_{\mathrm{fatal}}); other warnings are kept in the payload without penalty. A blocking execution failure short-circuits downstream verification.

Text.

Text is extracted from the candidate HTML with script and style nodes removed; no reference OCR enters this verifier. Each required string is checked by case-sensitive substring presence after NFKC and punctuation normalization. The binary match is multiplied by two factors computed from the rendered text boxes: the ratio of their union to their summed area, which penalizes overlap, and their mean visible fraction inside the canvas.

Boundary.

Boundary combines two sub-scores computed from browser bounding boxes. The containment term is the fraction of overflowing element area that still falls inside the canvas,

Sovf=∑e∈𝒪area⁡(e∩C)∑e∈𝒪area⁡(e),S_{\mathrm{ovf}}=\frac{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{O}}\operatorname{area}(e\cap C)}{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{O}}\operatorname{area}(e)}, (D1)

where CC is the declared canvas and 𝒪\mathcal{O} collects elements whose horizontal or vertical excess exceeds 88 or 2424 pixels; hidden nodes, decorative elements, and SVG primitives are excluded. The shape term compares the rendered aspect ratio rI^r_{\hat{I}} with the declared rrefr_{\mathrm{ref}},

Ssize=exp⁡(−λ​|rI^−rref|rref),λ=2.5,S_{\mathrm{size}}=\exp\!\left(-\lambda\,\frac{\lvert r_{\hat{I}}-r_{\mathrm{ref}}\rvert}{r_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right),\qquad\lambda=2.5, (D2)

and the channel is their mean, sbdry=12​(Sovf+Ssize)s_{\mathrm{bdry}}=\tfrac{1}{2}(S_{\mathrm{ovf}}+S_{\mathrm{size}}). The two terms capture unrelated failures: a page can match the canvas shape while spilling a table past its lower edge, or keep every element inside a canvas of the wrong proportions.

Table and chart.

Tables are parsed from HTML, and each expected row is greedily matched to an unused candidate row regardless of order. Numeric cells require normalized equality, while other cells may match by normalized alphanumeric containment; the table score is the fraction of expected rows reproduced. Charts are read from live ECharts series, falling back to static script extraction. When a chart subtype is required, data and subtype contribute 60%60\% and 40%40\%. Both branches are multiplied by the mean in-canvas visible fraction of the elements. The record stores field-level matches, so a correct chart type with wrong values can be told apart from a missing chart (Figure D2). The channel is not applicable when the prompt requires neither a table nor a chart.

Semantic layout.

SemanticLayout compares where content lands rather than how it is styled. PaddleOCR extracts text boxes from the reference and candidate renders, with candidate DOM boxes as a fallback, and adjacent fragments are merged. For each reference block, candidates with SequenceMatcher similarity below 0.30.3 are discarded and the spatially closest remaining one is selected. A matched pair jj with centre distance djd_{j} in normalized canvas units receives

proxj=exp⁡(−dj22​σ2),σ=0.15.\operatorname{prox}_{j}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{d_{j}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),\qquad\sigma=0.15. (D3)

Writing ℳ\mathcal{M} for the matched pairs and 𝒱ref\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ref}} for the merged reference blocks, so that ρ=|ℳ|/|𝒱ref|\rho=\lvert\mathcal{M}\rvert/\lvert\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ref}}\rvert is the match rate, the channel is

slayout=(1|ℳ|​∑j∈ℳproxj)​(0.9+0.1​ρ).s_{\mathrm{layout}}=\left(\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{M}\rvert}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}}\operatorname{prox}_{j}\right)\bigl(0.9+0.1\,\rho\bigr). (D4)

Colour, typeface, and exact box extent do not enter the score, so a candidate may diverge stylistically but not spatially (Figure D3).

Whitespace.

We extract a content mask from each screenshot by combining Canny edges with pixels whose intensity differs by more than 2525 from the median border intensity, and rasterize it into coarse (12×812\times 8) and fine (24×1624\times 16) occupancy grids. Each image is gridded in its own pixel space, so a different render size is not itself penalized. With flattened grids 𝐠c\mathbf{g}^{c} and 𝐠f\mathbf{g}^{f},

sws=12cos(𝐠I^c,𝐠Irefc)+12cos(𝐠I^f,𝐠Ireff).s_{\mathrm{ws}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\cos\!\left(\mathbf{g}^{c}_{\hat{I}},\mathbf{g}^{c}_{I_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)+\tfrac{1}{2}\cos\!\left(\mathbf{g}^{f}_{\hat{I}},\mathbf{g}^{f}_{I_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right). (D5)

The coarse grid captures global visual mass, and the fine grid remains sensitive to local crowding and empty regions (Figure D4).

Visual Graph Rubric

GPT-5.5 turns each reference into a rubric in two calls. The first reads the generation prompt and the reference and returns a layout class together with a scene graph of nodes and edges. The second receives that graph with the same prompt and image and writes yes/no questions, each bound to a node, an edge, a set of nodes, or the whole canvas, and typed as structure, completeness, visual attribute, relation, subgraph, forbidden, or global. Fixing the graph before the questions are written keeps the structure a question refers to from drifting, and lets every question cite the element it tests. Textual fidelity is excluded, since the Text verifier handles it. At scoring time GPT-5.5 answers the fixed rubric from the candidate rendering alone, and the reward is

svgr=1|Q|∑q∈Q[aq(I^)=paq].s_{\mathrm{vgr}}=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\mathbb{1}\!\left[a_{q}(\hat{I})=\operatorname{pa}_{q}\right]. (D6)

Each stored predicate keeps its type, binding, question, pass-answer polarity, model answer, and pass flag, so we can see which criterion changes between two rollouts even when their aggregate scores are similar.

Three rules of the templates carry most of the behavior we rely on. First, the layout class (free form, symmetric grid, timeline sequence, hub and spoke, or hierarchical) is committed before any question is written and sets the subgraph quota, because a forced subgraph question on a flat grid is only a row-alignment question under a graph label. Second, repeated identical elements are folded into one group node with a count, so four KPI cards produce one layout predicate rather than four existence checks. Third, opaque image and icon slots are addressed only by their geometry and position, never by their depicted content, because the reference generator may draw a different picture in the same slot and a content question would penalize a difference the prompt never specified. A programmatic linter checks every rubric for missing bindings, inconsistent polarity, and questions about text or image content; over the 7,4087{,}408 training rubrics it flags 2020 (0.3%0.3\%), and 99.6%99.6\% of questions bind to an element of their own graph. The template asks for 1010 to 2020 questions, and realized rubrics average 14.114.1 (range 1212–1919).

The judge answers the whole list in one call, which keeps the cost of the channel independent of rubric length. It sees only the candidate rendering and the questions, never the reference: the reference enters the reward only through the questions authored from it, which keeps the channel from degenerating into an image-similarity score. Two complete rubrics follow.

Appendix E Evaluation Protocol and Human Study

The final benchmark does not reuse the reference-conditioned SemanticLayout, Whitespace, or VGR rewards of Appendix D; every reported score is computed from the prompt and the candidate rendering alone. Rule averages the prompt-derived Text, Boundary, and Table/Chart scores, and 8989 of the 300300 prompts carry at least one table or chart requirement. Visual is produced by the checklist pipeline below. Because both Visual and the training rubric rest on model judgments, the section closes with a blinded human study that audits them.

Visual Checklist

Checklist questions are authored from the prompt and its parsed requirements, and proposals that are ambiguous, not decidable from a rendering, or that prescribe a particular implementation are discarded. The pipeline was developed on a separate 50-instance set that does not overlap the benchmark, then frozen and applied unchanged to the 300300 benchmark items. The frozen checklists contain 10,72710{,}727 questions, of which 1,9251{,}925 are Content, 4,5654{,}565 Layout, and 4,2374{,}237 Style, with 2626–5050 questions per prompt (mean 35.835.8). Each question is answered from the candidate rendering, a dimension score is the pass rate of its questions, and Visual is the mean of the available dimensions; the two prompts with no Content question have that dimension excluded rather than scored zero.

Every question names the element it is about, is decidable from a single rendering, and carries a kind label that maps to one dimension. Content collects kinds that ask whether a required element is present and intact, such as located presence, element count, and element integrity. Layout collects kinds about how elements sit relative to one another or to the canvas, such as collision, containment, structure, and page balance. Style collects kinds about the quality of rendering, such as element quality, icon quality, concrete attribute, and page density. Per-kind quotas keep a page from being scored almost entirely on whether its strings are present. The contract each question must satisfy is given below.

A small number of whole-page Style questions are written as disqualifier lists, in which any one of several defects fails the page; the delivery-gate questions in Section E.1 are of this form. They ask whether the page clears a publication bar at all, so splitting them would report one verdict several times. They bind to the canvas, and all element-level questions follow the atomicity rule.

At scoring time the frozen checklist is answered one category at a time over the same image, so the judge has a single decision criterion per call. We reproduce the judging template in full. Three of its provisions matter for reading the numbers. The canvas is fixed, so an element that runs past the edge counts as lost content, while full-bleed bands that merely touch the edge are not defects. Placeholder boxes are required by our prompts and count as the image being present, the evaluation-side counterpart of the opaque-slot rule in Section D.4. Every answer must cite the region it was read from, and an answer that cannot is recorded as unclear and scored as a failure, so a property the judge cannot verify does not silently pass.

The brief substituted at {brief} is the only part of the prompt that changes between calls, and it states the standard of proof for its category. The relation and style briefs demand a higher standard than completeness, because those are the categories where a page that merely looks orderly is easiest to mistake for one that satisfies the question.

A complete checklist.

This example reproduces all 33 evaluation questions for one instance, covering Content, Layout, and Style. It was selected for legible policy and metric groups, not model scores. Figure E1 shows the prompt and an image illustrating the subject matter.

H locates the title block; G, the section heading; P1–P3, the three policy pillars; and S1–S3, the subsidy, drug-directory, and cross-provincial-settlement groups. Canvas means the whole page. These are manual reading aids for this figure, not additional graph bindings or layout requirements in the evaluator. Question IDs, dimension assignments, and pass polarities are retained from the records; “Pass” states the required answer and does not report a model outcome.

Style: shared judging instruction for DG01–DG05

Judge this against finished professional design work, the standard of a studio’s released output. Do not judge it against the other attempts you have seen, and do not judge it as a hunt for mistakes. A page can contain no outright error and still be a long way from that standard. Being plain, safe, generic or underdeveloped is not neutral here: it means the work is unfinished, and a page with little on it has more design left to do, not less.

The preceding instruction is an identical prefix in each of DG01–DG05; it is printed once here. Each complete question is that prefix followed by its row below. No question text is omitted.

External Benchmark Protocols

We evaluate Design2Code, SlidesBench, and GDB/lica under their official protocols. Design2Code measures block matching, text similarity, position, color, and CLIP similarity against the target webpage, and generations that fail to render receive zero. SlidesBench scores content, layout, and color on a 0–5 scale. For GDB/lica we report NIMA, CLIP, PickScore, FID, color harmony, and OCR fidelity, where OCR is the fraction of ground-truth tokens recovered by Tesseract (page segmentation mode 6) after the benchmark’s normalization; on the same 100 renders it gives 0.719, 0.561, and 0.685 for GPT-5.5, Qwen3-VL-32B, and AesCode-32B. All rows of Table 2 are run by us with one decoding, rendering, and scoring pipeline per benchmark, so scores are comparable across systems within a benchmark but not across benchmarks.

Human Study on Our Benchmark

We recruited 52 participants and retained 150 completed questionnaires after quality control; questionnaires completed by the same participant contain disjoint items, and all participants gave informed consent. Each questionnaire has 35–36 formal items, namely six judge-reliability, 10–11 Content, three or four aesthetic, and 16 consistency items, plus an instruction check and an obvious visual sentinel. Every formal item is judged by three different participants. Block and item order are counterbalanced, and system identity, automatic scores, machine answers, and reference images are hidden. Incomplete sessions, failed checks, and image-loading failures are excluded independently of response direction, and uncertainty estimates account for repeated observations within sessions and briefs.

Judge reliability.

This study asks whether people reproduce the local decisions of the automatic judges. We sample 150 predicates each from the training VGR and the Visual checklist, stratified by dimension. Each page shows one candidate image and one predicate, answered Yes, No, or Unclear, and the automatic answer is compared with the three-person majority. For the automatic judge, Unclear is a failure because every answer must cite evidence; for people, Unclear is missing, since abstaining is not asserting that a property is absent. Agreement is therefore computed over predicates whose human majority is Yes or No.

Content and aesthetic quality.

This study tests whether AesCode-32B satisfies more explicit Content requirements than GPT-5.5 while matching its aesthetic quality. The Content task covers all 267 eligible briefs with one frozen image per system: of the 300 briefs, 30 are reserved for the pilot that fixed the protocol, two have no Content question, and one lacks a complete set of GPT-5.5 renders. Participants see the brief, one image, and its Content questions; the two systems appear on separate pages, and no session contains both versions of a brief. Responses are averaged within question and then within image, with Unclear treated as missing. The aesthetic task shows one image from each system for 80 briefs, without the brief or checklist, and asks for a 1–7 rating. Equivalence requires the entire 95% confidence interval of the difference to lie within the pre-specified [−0.5,+0.5][-0.5,+0.5] margin.

Score–preference consistency.

This study asks whether Visual scores predict human preference. Five images for each of 80 briefs form ten within-brief pairs. Participants see one anonymized pair without the brief and choose A better, B better, Tie, or Unclear; each pair receives three judgments with balanced left–right order. For pairs with unequal scores, choosing the higher-scoring image counts 1, Tie 0.5, and the lower-scoring image 0, with Unclear missing. Equal-score pairs are reported separately, and agreement is broken down by score gap.

Human Study on External Benchmarks

We additionally collect 50 completed questionnaires of 16 or 17 pairwise items for Design2Code, SlidesBench, and GDB/lica. For each benchmark, the eight evaluated systems form 28 model pairs, from each of which we freeze two score-blind, same-task comparisons, giving 56 image pairs per benchmark and 168 overall; every pair is judged five times, for 840 judgments. Each page shows two anonymized outputs and asks which is more aesthetically polished, with the task, reference, system identity, and scores hidden.

Each benchmark is summarized by a per-sample composite. Design2Code averages Block, Text, Position, Color, and CLIP; SlidesBench averages Content, Layout, and Color; GDB/lica averages normalized NIMA, CLIP, PickScore, Color Harmony, OCR, and a reversed paired feature distance, since FID is defined only over a set of images. Agreement is scored as above and averaged first within and then across pairs. To compare gaps across scales we use 100​|sA−sB|/R100|s_{A}-s_{B}|/R, where RR is the metric range, grouped into <5<5, 55–1515, and ≥15\geq 15; confidence intervals use a source-task cluster bootstrap (Table E5).

Appendix F Failure Analysis

Section 4.4 names three residual failure modes. This appendix measures them and analyzes why the relational and semantic modes persist. All measurements use the 300300-prompt benchmark and the three judged rollouts of Table 1.

Measuring the three modes

A failure is recurrent when it appears in at least two of the three rollouts for a prompt. Boundary applies to every page and is measured over all 300300 prompts. The other two modes apply only to prompts that call for a connected structure or for semantic elements such as icons, so they are measured over the 4646 and 3030 prompts whose checklist contains the corresponding predicate. Table F1 reports the rates, and Figure F1 shows two further instances of each mode.

On Boundary, the paired difference to GPT-5.5 is −30.3-30.3 points ([−36.0,−24.7][-36.0,-24.7]). The residual cases share a shape. The dashboard in Figure 5 fails in all three rollouts: its two lower panels begin at y=535y=535 px and each request 410410 px of height on a 720720 px canvas. Every region is constructed, but independent fixed-pixel allocations exceed the page height, and the running total is the one quantity that stays invisible until the page is rendered.

Why the relational and semantic modes persist

Relational structure is supervised explicitly. The design graph carries order, connection, and hierarchy edges such as timeline_step, connects, and parent_of, the layout class sets a subgraph quota, and VGR binds relation- and subgraph-type predicates to these edges (Section D.4). The mode persists because it is the hardest objective to optimize, for two reasons.

First, credit for a relation is implicit. A relation predicate is one of about fourteen rubric questions whose pass rate forms a single channel, and GDPO normalizes per channel rather than per question, so the advantage of a violated relation is shared with every other criterion on the page. Subgraph-level supervision is also sparse and coarse: only 4646 of the 10,72710{,}727 checklist predicates are subgraph-level, and a failed one marks the page rather than the responsible edge.

Second, the objective is intrinsically demanding. On the 4646 relational prompts, pairwise relation predicates pass at 95.3%95.3\% and local structure predicates at 95.8%95.8\%, while the whole-subgraph predicate passes at 75.4%75.4\%. Drawing nodes and local arrangements is local and readily learned; holding a timeline, hierarchy, or branch set together as one connected object requires knowledge of the content, reasoning over it, and planning the global layout around it. GPT-5.5 shows the same ordering, so the difficulty lies in the predicate type rather than in our pipeline. The five-link example in Figure 5 illustrates this: every link element exists, and one shared geometry rule removes every vertical stroke at once.

Semantic elements fail at a similar level of abstraction. In Figure 5, the controls sit in plausible slots with a consistent treatment, yet a phone, camera, gear, beaker, atom, or monitor becomes hard to tell apart. Rendering a recognizable icon means mapping a meaning to a drawn form in fine-grained SVG, which draws on the visual knowledge of the backbone. Our rewards supervise the slot’s presence, geometry, and treatment, and by design leave its depicted content unscored, because the reference generator may draw a different picture in the same slot (Section D.4).
